notes:
I couldn't get everything for this passage. The Enduring Word page cut off partway through v. 25. I found nothing from the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Pentecostal or modern-scholarship sites, and nothing that describes prosperity or word-of-faith teaching on the widow by name. I've left those out rather than fill the gaps. The only Catholic voice below is Cornelius a Lapide, a Catholic commentator whose work I read on studylight.org.

## Mark 12:23–44: Research notes

**v. 23**
- The Sadducees asked the question to make the resurrection look absurd. They were wealthy and influential and didn't believe in immortality, spirits or angels. The Law of Moses (Deut 25:5–6) set up "levirate marriage": if a man died childless, his brother married the widow so the dead man would have an heir. Guzik (Enduring Word) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-12/
- They mean to blame Moses, since his own command produced the woman with seven husbands. Asking "whose wife" carries a quiet sarcasm. The Expositor's Bible https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/mark-12.html

**v. 24**
- Jesus names two causes of their error: they don't know the Scriptures, which anchor belief, and they don't know God's power, so they doubt He can do what He promised. Guzik https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-12/

**v. 25**
- The Sadducees assumed resurrection life would be this life continued. Jesus says the coming age runs on a completely different principle, and heaven is not just a better earth. Guzik https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-12/
- Matthew Henry: marriage began in the earthly paradise but will not exist in the heavenly one. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/12-25.html
- Gill: no such natural relationship will exist, and none will be needed. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/leb/mark/12-25.html
- People will not become angels. They will share the angels' freedom from death and from marriage. https://biblehub.com/matthew/22-30.htm
- "Like the angels" means being like them in some respects (deathless, close to God). It does not mean turning into angels. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_no_marriage_in_heaven_Mark_12_25.htm

**v. 26**
- Henry's Concise Commentary: if Abraham were gone for ever, the living God could not be his portion, so Abraham's soul must still exist. biblehub https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-26.htm
- Poole: Jesus could have quoted clearer texts from Job, Daniel or Ezekiel. He chose Moses because the Sadducees accepted those books. biblehub https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-26.htm
- Ligonier: the argument rests on both the verb tense and theology. If death had ended the patriarchs, God would have said "I *was*." Ligonier https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/god-of-living
- John Piper takes a different angle. He says the stress falls on the word *God*, not on "am": if God is your God, His power means death cannot rob you of life. Desiring God https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/lord-of-the-dead
- Coffman quotes F. C. Grant: the strongest argument for immortality is the character of God, not human nature. studylight https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/12-26.html
- **The sources disagree here.** Chuck Smith says the Sadducees rejected everything in the Old Testament except the five books of Moses. studylight https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/12-25.html. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the New Testament gives no basis for that view, and Josephus only says they rejected Pharisee traditions. biblehub https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-27.htm

**v. 27**
- Gill: because God is still their God, the patriarchs' souls are alive now. Their bodies must also rise, or He would not be the God of the whole person. biblehub https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-27.htm
- Coffman notes three things: Jesus treats the Pentateuch as God's word, rests the resurrection on one verb tense, and shows the patriarchs are in some sense living. studylight https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/12-27.html

**v. 28**
- Unlike the earlier questioners, this scribe didn't try to trap Jesus with politics or mock the afterlife. He asked a sincere question. Hastings https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hastings/mark/12-34.htm

**vv. 29–31**
- Jesus quotes the Shema (Deut 6:4–5), Judaism's basic creed, which devout Jews say every morning and evening. H. B. Charles https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/charles_hb/articles/devotional/the-most-important-commandment.cfm
- D. A. Carson notes that Jesus starts with the Shema itself, God's identity, before giving any command. TGC https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/on-loving-god-with-all-your-mind/
- Henry: where love for God rules the soul, the heart is ready for every other duty. biblehub https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-34.htm
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) says the Hebrew word for "one" (*echad*) means a compound unity. studylight https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/12-29.html
- Love for others grows out of love for God, which is why Jesus puts the two commands together. GotQuestions https://www.gotquestions.org/not-far-from-the-kingdom-of-God.html

**vv. 32–33**
- The scribe sees that God wants changed hearts more than outward ritual. Bridgeway https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/12-29.html
- His reply echoes Hosea 6:6. biblehub https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_Mark_12_34_s_kingdom_phrase.htm

**v. 34: where traditions differ most in this section**
- **Calvin (Reformed):** two reasons. The scribe was easily persuaded to do his duty, and he could tell outward worship apart from essential duties. studylight https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/12-34.html
- **Carson (Reformed, TGC):** Jesus doesn't mean you get in by obeying. Read in light of Mark 10:45, the commands show us our need, and entry comes through Jesus' death for our sins. TGC https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/first-commandment-first-sin-mark-12-28-34/
- **Gill (Calvinist Baptist):** this isn't about nearness to heaven. Knowing or keeping commands can't bring a sinner there, since heaven is a pure gift of grace. The scribe was near the *gospel age*. biblehub https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-34.htm
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** the scribe's openness and his break from trust in outward worship put him near. Spurgeon urges hearers to stop trying to save themselves and let Jesus save them. studylight https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/12-34.html
- **Adam Clarke (Methodist):** he was almost a Christian, close enough to step in easily, and probably did come to believe later. studylight https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/12-34.html
- **Pulpit Commentary (Anglican):** he was near "the Church militant here on earth," the way to the Church in heaven, but still lacked faith in Christ. biblehub https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-34.htm
- **Ellicott:** as in the Sermon on the Mount, recognising the righteousness that fulfils the law brings a person to the kingdom's threshold. biblehub https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-34.htm
- **Common warning:** "not far" still means outside. H. B. Charles https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/charles_hb/articles/devotional/the-most-important-commandment.cfm

**vv. 35–36**
- Mark sets this question before the people. Matthew presents it as the closing challenge to the Pharisees. Meyer (in the Expositor's Greek Testament) says Mark's version looks original. biblehub https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-35.htm
- Meyer also says the verse doesn't spell out Jesus' pre-existence. "By the Holy Spirit" only means David spoke as a prophet. biblehub https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-35.htm
- Barclay: Psalm 110 is the Old Testament passage the New Testament quotes most. studylight https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/12-35.html
- Most ancient Jewish interpreters read the psalm as about the Messiah. biblehub sermons https://biblehub.com/sermons/mark/12-35.htm

**v. 37**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the Messiah is lower than David as his son in the flesh, and higher as Lord of the kingdom David belongs to. biblehub https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-37.htm
- Gill: Jesus was showing that the Messiah is God as well as man. studylight https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/12-37.html
- Constable quotes Bailey: only the virgin birth gives Jesus the two natures that make Him both David's Son and David's Lord. The crowd's delight underlines Jesus' authority. studylight https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/12-37.html

**vv. 38–40**
- The scribes' prayers were a pretence. Under cover of religion they took what should have supported people with no one to help them. The Expositor's Bible https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/mark-12.html
- Coffman: they did it through excessive fees and by abusing people's hospitality. studylight https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/mark-12.html
- Lapide (Catholic): they demanded lavish meals and took money in exchange for promising to pray for widows. studylight https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/clc/mark-12.html
- Henry: hidden sin is double sin, and hypocrites face the heaviest judgment. studylight https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/mark-12.html

**vv. 41–42**
- The rich may have been making a show of their giving. Guzik https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-12/
- Mark translates the coin's value into a Roman coin (the quadrans) for his Roman readers. Guzik https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-12/
- Bengel: she could have kept one of the two coins. biblehub https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-42.htm
- Ellicott: she belongs to the group just described as having their houses devoured, yet she kept the two great commandments. biblehub https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-42.htm
- The BSB study notes link her to the widow of Zarephath (1 Kings 17). biblehub https://biblehub.com/mark/12-42.htm

**vv. 43–44: a real disagreement about the widow**
- **Traditional reading: Jesus praises her sacrifice.**
  - Guzik: what a gift costs the giver sets its value. Enduring Word https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-12/
  - Henry: many would criticise her, but Christ commends her, so she did well. blueletterbible https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_012.cfm
  - Lapide (Catholic), citing Thomas Aquinas and Ambrose: God looks less at the gift than at the giver's heart. studylight https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/clc/mark-12.html
  - Coffman: the poor should give too, and poverty is no excuse not to. studylight https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/mark-12.html
- **Lament reading (GotQuestions):**
  - Jesus never tells anyone to copy her, never praises her faith, and never promises God will pay her back. GotQuestions https://www.gotquestions.org/widows-mite.html
  - Coming straight after v. 40, she is an example of what Jesus had just condemned: a religious system that takes everything from the vulnerable. GotQuestions https://www.gotquestions.org/widows-mite.html
  - Henry also raises the worry that the chief priests handled the treasury unfairly, though he still sides with Jesus' praise. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_012.cfm
- **Popular misuse:** Coffman calls this one of the most misused passages in the New Testament. People "give their mite" meaning a small amount, not everything they have. studylight https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/mark-12.html. A Davies quote in Ellicott's notes on biblehub makes a similar point about calling a cheap gift a "mite." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-42.htm
